passage: In the colony park in Ludhiana, Gurleen climbed the low slide while her mother Minakshi sat on the bench. Halfway up, Gurleen looked back. Minakshi waved. Gurleen slid down, tripped on the grass and scraped her palm. She ran straight to the bench, holding her hand out. Minakshi blew on it and held her until the crying stopped. Then Gurleen slipped off her lap and ran back to the slide, glancing once at the bench.

qa.q: Where was Minakshi sitting while Gurleen played?
qa.a: Minakshi sat on the bench in the colony park.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen look back at the bench halfway up the slide?
qa.a: She wanted to check that her mother was still there, and seeing Minakshi wave made her feel safe to keep going.

qa.q: How does Minakshi's steady presence support Gurleen's play?
qa.a: Because Minakshi stays in view and comforts her quickly when she is hurt, Gurleen feels secure enough to go back and explore on her own.

qa.q: What would change if Minakshi often walked away without Gurleen knowing?
qa.a: Gurleen might stop exploring and cling instead, because she could no longer count on her mother being there when she needed her.

grounding: Shows a toddler's trust that her caregiver will be there to meet her needs, which lets her explore.

passage:
"Mama?" Varun's voice came from the cot in the dark.
"I'm here, jaan," said Salma, turning on the small lamp.
"Milk."
"Milk is coming. Let me warm it."
Varun sat up, holding the cot bars, and watched the door. He didn't cry.
"Here it is." She sat on the floor beside him while he drank.
"Mama stay."
"I'll stay till you're sleepy."
He handed back the cup, lay down and curled his fingers round her thumb.

qa.q: What did Varun ask for when he woke?
qa.a: He asked for milk.

qa.q: Why didn't Varun cry while waiting for the milk?
qa.a: He seems sure from experience that when Salma says milk is coming, it really will come, so he can wait calmly.

qa.q: What in Salma's replies builds Varun's sense of security?
qa.a: She answers him right away, tells him exactly what will happen and then does it, so her words and actions match.

qa.q: What might Salma feel as Varun curls his fingers round her thumb?
qa.a: She would likely feel tired but tender, knowing her steady care is what lets him settle back to sleep. ❤️

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's secure trust that his caregiver will meet his physical and emotional needs.

passage:
Monthly note on Payal, from Asif at the day-care.
When Payal joined in June, she screamed at drop-off and wouldn't let me hold her. I kept to the same steps every day: greet her at the gate, offer her the blue cushion, snack after circle time.
By now she waves bye to her father and toddles in. When she's hungry, she comes and taps the snack shelf, then waits. Yesterday she fell asleep on my arm during story. 😊

qa.q: What did Payal do at drop-off when she first joined in June?
qa.a: She screamed at drop-off and wouldn't let Asif hold her.

qa.q: What does Payal tapping the snack shelf and then waiting suggest she believes?
qa.a: It suggests she now believes Asif will notice and give her food, so she trusts her need will be met without crying.

qa.q: Which of Asif's habits helped Payal settle in?
qa.a: Doing the same steps every day, from greeting her at the gate to snack after circle time, made the day predictable and let her trust Asif.

qa.q: How might Payal's father feel reading this note?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and grateful that she has gone from screaming at drop-off to waving bye and resting on Asif's arm. 🙏

grounding: Shows a toddler building secure trust that a consistent caregiver will meet her needs.

passage: In the wheat field's shade, Amandeep woke from his nap on the charpai and called out, 'Ammi!' Dilnaz, cutting grass nearby, straightened and waved. 'Here, jaan.' He sat up, sucked his thumb, and watched her. When a buffalo lowed, he called again, and again she answered and came to rub his back. Soon he climbed down and lined up pebbles, glancing now and then to find her still there.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz doing when Amandeep woke?
qa.a: She was cutting grass nearby in the field.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep keep glancing at Dilnaz while he played?
qa.a: He wanted to check she was still there; knowing she would answer made him feel safe enough to play.

qa.q: What does Dilnaz's response show about building trust?
qa.a: Answering every call, even small ones, teaches him that his needs will be met, which lets him explore on his own.

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz often ignored his calls?
qa.a: He might cling more or cry longer, because he could not be sure she would come when he needed her.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's growing sense of security from a caregiver who responds consistently.

passage: At two in the morning, rain drummed on the flat's window in Hamburg. Hiroshi woke up and cried. Within a minute Elif was at the cot, her hair messy. 'I'm here. Just rain.' She laid a warm hand on his tummy. He hiccupped, found her finger and gripped it. His eyes closed slowly. Elif stayed a while, then tiptoed out. Hiroshi stirred once, then went back to sleep.

qa.q: What woke Hiroshi at two in the morning?
qa.a: Rain drumming on the window woke him, and he cried.

qa.q: What does Hiroshi gripping Elif's finger suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt comforted and safe with her there, and could relax back into sleep.

qa.q: What is helpful about how Elif responded?
qa.a: She came quickly and calmly and used touch and a few soft words, which is a steady, predictable comfort.

qa.q: What is it like for Elif to get up for these wakings?
qa.a: It may be tiring for her, but she seems to accept it and still stays until he settles. 😴

grounding: Shows a toddler feeling secure because a caregiver reliably meets his needs at night, set in Germany.

passage: I'm Jasleen, and I jog in the colony park most evenings. There's a little girl, Urmila, maybe two, who comes with her father. He sits on the same bench every day, and she wanders to the sandpit, then the slide, looking back at him every few minutes. When she tripped yesterday, she didn't even cry until she'd run all the way to him. He picked her up, blew on her knee, and she went straight back to the slide.

qa.q: Where does Urmila's father sit?
qa.a: On the same bench every day.

qa.q: What does Urmila's habit of looking back at her father suggest?
qa.a: She feels safe knowing he is there, so she can explore and still check in.

qa.q: What is Urmila's father doing that supports her trust?
qa.a: He is in the same spot every time and comforts her quickly, so she learns she can count on him.

qa.q: How does Jasleen read the moment when Urmila fell?
qa.a: Jasleen notices she held her tears until she reached her father, and guesses he is her safe place.

grounding: Shows a toddler exploring with confidence because her father is reliably there, seen by a park regular.

passage: Night one in the new flat: Dolma, twenty months, woke three times and screamed until her father Sumit came. Each time he picked her up and said, "Papa's here." Night four: she woke once, called "Papa?" softly, heard his voice from the next room, and lay back down. Night ten: she woke, turned over, hugged her cloth rabbit and went back to sleep on her own.

qa.q: What did Sumit say each time he picked Dolma up?
qa.a: He said, "Papa's here."

qa.q: What does Dolma lying back down after hearing Sumit's voice suggest?
qa.a: She felt reassured and secure, trusting he was near even without seeing him.

qa.q: Why did Sumit's steady response help Dolma settle?
qa.a: Coming every time taught her that her needs would be met, so she felt safe enough to need him less.

qa.q: What is it like for Sumit during those first nights?
qa.a: It is exhausting to get up three times, but seeing her settle by night ten would feel rewarding.

grounding: Shows a toddler's trust growing over several nights as her father answers her every time.

passage: On the third night of Navratri the society courtyard in Ahmedabad was packed with dancers. Swati, two, sat on her mother Tanuja's hip, watching the swirling skirts. When Tanuja set her down, Swati gripped her dupatta, then let go to clap along. Every few minutes she spun round to find her mother's face, and Tanuja always waved back. Near midnight, tired and sweaty, Swati lifted her arms, and Tanuja picked her up without a word.

qa.q: Which night of Navratri was it?
qa.a: The third night.

qa.q: What does Swati letting go of the dupatta to clap suggest?
qa.a: She felt secure enough, knowing her mother was close, to join in on her own.

qa.q: What small habit of Tanuja's helps Swati feel safe in a crowd?
qa.a: Waving back every time Swati looks for her, and picking her up the moment she asks.

qa.q: How might Tanuja experience the night?
qa.a: She gets to enjoy the dancing while staying alert to Swati, and feels glad her daughter explores a little.

grounding: Shows a toddler feeling secure enough to explore a festival crowd because her mother responds every time.

passage:
"Papa!" Mohit, twenty months, called into the dark. The winter wind rattled the window.
"Coming, Mohit." Footsteps. Suraj sat on the bed. "Cold?"
"Co'."
"Here, blanket." He tucked it up to Mohit's chin. "Water?"
Mohit nodded. Suraj brought the steel cup, and Mohit drank, holding it with both hands.
"Papa here?"
"Papa here. Papa always comes."
Mohit put his hand on Suraj's arm, sighed, and closed his eyes. His fingers stayed there till he slept.

qa.q: What did Suraj bring Mohit to drink from?
qa.a: The steel cup.

qa.q: What does Mohit keeping his hand on Suraj's arm suggest?
qa.a: Mohit felt safe and secure, trusting that Papa is there.

qa.q: What makes Suraj's night response build Mohit's trust?
qa.a: He comes every time, meets each need, warmth and water, and says calmly that Papa always comes.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel as Mohit falls asleep holding his arm?
qa.a: Suraj probably feels tender and content, seeing how much Mohit relies on him.

grounding: On a windy winter night, a toddler calls and his father comes, meeting his needs and deepening his trust.

passage: Creche note, the week after Losar. For weeks Tenzin (2) used to cry at drop-off. His mother always said the same words, "Amala comes after snack and song," and she always came at five. Today he waved at the door and went to the blocks, and at five he looked up at the gate before she even arrived. When she came, he ran to her, then went back to finish his tower. I'll tell her how settled he is. — Arohi

qa.q: What time did Tenzin's mother always come?
qa.a: At five.

qa.q: What does Tenzin going back to finish his tower suggest?
qa.a: Tenzin felt secure and calm, trusting his mother would be there, so he could keep playing.

qa.q: What built Tenzin's trust at drop-off?
qa.a: His mother's same words each time and always coming when promised, which made the pattern predictable.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's mother feel reading the note?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and proud that her consistency has helped him settle.

grounding: A creche note after Losar shows a toddler who trusts his mother's reliable return.

passage: In paddy-planting season, Mehak worked in the flooded fields near their village in Mandya from dawn. Vijay, twenty months, stayed with his Ajji on the verandah. Every day at noon, Mehak came back along the bund, muddy to the knees, and called, "Vijay!" This week, when the noon siren sounded from the rice mill, Vijay stopped playing, toddled to the edge of the verandah, and looked towards the bund, sure. There she was. He clapped.

qa.q: Where did Mehak work in planting season?
qa.a: In the flooded fields near their village.

qa.q: What does Vijay toddling to the edge at the siren suggest?
qa.a: Vijay felt sure and eager, trusting his mother would come at noon as always.

qa.q: What helped Vijay feel secure while his mother worked?
qa.a: Mehak returning at the same time every day and calling his name, with Ajji caring for him meanwhile.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel seeing Vijay waiting for her?
qa.a: Mehak would likely feel warmth and joy, seeing his trust in her return.

grounding: In rice-planting season, a toddler trusts that his mother will return from the fields at noon as she always does.

passage:
The rainy season in Addis Ababa meant muddy courtyards. Abebe, two, was chasing a hen when he slipped and landed hard on his bottom.

He didn't cry at once. He looked straight at his father on the step.

Tariq was already coming. "I'm here." He lifted Abebe, checked his hands and knees, and rubbed his back.

Abebe sniffed, then pointed at the hen and wriggled to be put down again.

qa.q: What was Abebe chasing?
qa.a: Abebe was chasing a hen.

qa.q: How was Abebe feeling when he looked at his father after falling?
qa.a: Abebe was shaken but trusting, looking to his father for comfort before crying.

qa.q: How did Tariq help Abebe feel safe?
qa.a: He came quickly, reassured him, checked for hurts, and let him go back to play.

qa.q: How might Tariq feel knowing Abebe looks to him first?
qa.a: Tariq would likely feel trusted and proud, knowing Abebe relies on him.

grounding: During the rainy season, a toddler trusts his father to comfort him after a fall and returns to play.

passage:
I'm Gargi, Tushar's cousin. At my didi's winter wedding, Tushar, who's about two, toddled off toward the buffet.

Every few steps, he looked back to find his mother. When he saw her, he kept going. When a guest blocked his view, he stopped until he could see her again.

After a while he ran back, touched her knee, and ran off again. I'm not sure what he was thinking, but he seemed to know she'd still be there.

qa.q: What did Tushar do every few steps?
qa.a: Every few steps, he looked back to find his mother.

qa.q: What might Tushar have been feeling as he explored the wedding?
qa.a: Gargi couldn't be sure, but Tushar seemed secure and curious, trusting his mother would stay nearby.

qa.q: How could Tushar's mother support his confidence in a crowded place?
qa.a: Stay in one spot where he can see her and smile when he looks back.

qa.q: How does Gargi see Tushar's checking back?
qa.a: Gargi notices it with interest, guessing he knows his mother will still be there.

grounding: A cousin watches a toddler at a winter wedding explore while checking back on his mother, showing trust in her presence.

passage:
First week in the new flat, deep winter: Pema, twenty months, wakes at night and screams. Chetan goes to her each time.

Two weeks later: she wakes and cries, but when she hears Chetan's footsteps, she stops and lies down.

On Losar night: Pema wakes, calls "Pa?" once, hears him say, "I'm here," from the next room, and goes back to sleep.

qa.q: What did Pema call on Losar night?
qa.a: She called "Pa?" once.

qa.q: How was Pema feeling by Losar night?
qa.a: Pema felt safe and settled, trusting that Chetan was close by.

qa.q: What helped Pema build trust in the new flat?
qa.a: Chetan came to her every time she woke, so she learned he would always respond.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel after weeks of night waking?
qa.a: Chetan might feel tired but relieved and happy to see Pema settle more easily.

grounding: Over a winter in a new home, a toddler comes to trust that her father will respond, and settles more easily at night.

passage: In their third-floor flat in Pune, Lalit woke from his nap and called, "Mumma!" From the kitchen came, "Coming, Lalit! Two minutes." He sat up on the bed with his thumb in his mouth and waited, not crying. His cousin Raghav, visiting for the day, peeped in. "He's not even scared," Raghav said. Mumma came, lifted Lalit and gave him water. Lalit tucked his head under her chin, then wriggled down to show Raghav his truck.

qa.q: What did Lalit's Mumma call from the kitchen?
qa.a: She called, "Coming, Lalit! Two minutes."

qa.q: Why did Lalit wait on the bed without crying?
qa.a: He felt secure, trusting that his Mumma would come when she said she would.

qa.q: How can Lalit's parents keep this trust growing?
qa.a: They can keep answering when he calls and doing what they say, such as coming when they promise.

qa.q: What is it like for Raghav to see Lalit so calm?
qa.a: Raghav is surprised, perhaps expecting a small child to be scared when waking up alone.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's secure trust that a caregiver will come when called.
